title: Title and occasion
short: Written for the London Musical Society's celebration of St Cecilia, patron saint of music, on 22 November 1687, with music by Giovanni Battista Draghi.
body: From the early 1680s a society of London musicians and amateurs held an annual feast on St Cecilia's Day (22 November), with a commissioned ode, a service and a dinner. Dryden's ode was set by Draghi, an Italian musician at the court of James II, and the text was later collected in Examen Poeticum (1693). Handel set it anew in 1739. The ode's design moves from the creation of the world by music, through the power of music over human passions (Jubal, the instruments), to St Cecilia's organ, and ends with music's role at the Last Judgement. Dryden had become a Catholic in 1685-86, and a saint's day ode under a Catholic king had a public dimension.

title: heavenly harmony ... universal frame
short: The ancient idea that the cosmos was made and is held together by harmony, here joined to the Christian account of creation by the divine Word.
body: Pythagorean and Platonic tradition (Plato's Timaeus, Boethius' musica mundana) held that the universe is ordered by musical proportion; Christian writers identified the creating 'tuneful voice' with God's Word (Genesis 1, John 1:1). 'Frame' means structure or fabric (OED), as in Hamlet's 'this goodly frame, the earth'. John Hollander's study of music in English poetry takes its title, The Untuning of the Sky, from the ode's last line. The refrain-like return of the opening lines mirrors the musical structure.

title: a heap / Of jarring atoms
short: Chaos is pictured as warring atoms, combining the Epicurean atomism of Lucretius with Ovid's chaos and the biblical creation.
body: Lucretius' De rerum natura describes a world formed by the chance collisions of atoms; Christian writers of the seventeenth century, wary of its atheism, recast atoms as raw material ordered by God. Ovid's account of creation (Metamorphoses 1.5-20) describes a 'rudis indigestaque moles', a crude unordered heap, in which the elements fought one another. Dryden borrows the 'heap' and the strife; 'jarring' is a musical word for discord, so chaos is literally untuned. Nature 'could not heave her head' until the creating voice called.

title: Arise, ye more than dead
short: The creating voice summons the inert elements as if waking the dead, anticipating the last trumpet of the Grand Chorus.
body: The elements are 'more than dead' because they have never lived. The command 'Arise' echoes the language of resurrection (compare 1 Corinthians 15 and Isaiah 26:19), so the first stanza's creation by sound already looks forward to the final stanza, where 'The trumpet shall be heard on high' and the dead shall live. The ode is thus framed by two sounding commands, at the beginning and the end of time.

title: cold, and hot, and moist
short: The four elementary qualities, whose combinations make the four elements; at music's command they leap into their ordered stations.
body: In Aristotelian physics, fire is hot and dry, air hot and moist, water cold and moist, earth cold and dry. Ovid's chaos is a war of these qualities ('frigida pugnabant calidis, umentia siccis', Metamorphoses 1.19). Dryden's line imitates the clash with its run of monosyllables joined by 'and', then resolves it as the qualities 'leap' into order, as if in a dance. The cosmos becomes a musical performance obeying 'Music's power'.

title: it rail (for 'ran')
short: The archive text reads 'it rail'; the early printings and modern editions read 'it ran', meaning the harmony ran through the whole range of notes.
body: The authoritative texts, from the 1687 broadside and Examen Poeticum (1693) onward, read 'Through all the compass of the notes it ran'. 'Rail' makes no sense here and is evidently a transcription error that has crept into this copy; readers should take the line as 'ran'. 'Compass' is the full range of an instrument or voice (OED), so the line describes creation as a scale rising through every note from the lowest creatures to the highest.

anchor: The diapason closing full in Man
title: diapason closing full in Man
greek: Greek he dia pason chordon 'through all the strings'
short: The diapason is the octave, the most perfect concord; creation runs up the scale and closes on Man, the last and fullest note.
body: Greek dia pason (chordon), 'through all the strings', named the octave, which completes the scale and returns to the keynote in perfect consonance. In Genesis 1 man is created last, and Renaissance thought made him a microcosm summing up all the lower orders of being. Dryden fuses the scale of music with the scale of nature (the chain of being): the 'closing' is both a musical cadence and the completion of creation. Johnson, in his Life of Dryden, praised the first stanza as vigorous and elegant but thought 'diapason' too technical a word.

title: What passion cannot Music raise
short: Stanza 2 turns from cosmic to human harmony: music's power to arouse and calm the passions, framed by the same question at start and close.
body: The idea that music moves the 'affections' was a commonplace from Plato and Aristotle to seventeenth-century musical theory, and it underlies the series of instruments and emotions in stanzas 3 to 5. The repeated question frames stanza 2 like a musical ritornello. Dryden returned to the theme a decade later in Alexander's Feast (1697), where Timotheus sways Alexander from pride to pity to love to rage.

title: Jubal ... chorded shell
short: Jubal, in Genesis 4:21 'the father of all such as handle the harp and organ'; his instrument is imagined as a lyre made from a tortoise shell.
body: Genesis 4:21 names Jubal, of the line of Cain, as the first musician. Dryden equips him with a 'chorded shell', the Greek lyre, which in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the infant god made by stringing a tortoise shell; Latin testudo means both tortoise and lyre. The biblical and classical myths of origin are thus fused. His brethren fall on their faces to worship the sound, believing a god must live in the shell: a hint that music's power can be mistaken for divinity, which the final stanza on Cecilia picks up with the angel 'mistaking earth for heaven'. (The RPO note gives Genesis 5:21, a misprint for 4:21.)

title: The trumpet's loud clangour; the drum
short: Stanzas 3 to 5 pair instruments with passions, and change metre and sound to imitate each: trumpet and drum for war, flute and lute for love, violins for jealousy.
body: Stanza 3 uses short, mostly anapaestic lines and harsh consonants for the trumpet, and the 'double double double beat' of the drum imitates the roll of the side drum, ending in the breathless command 'Charge, charge!'. 'Clangour' (from Latin clangor) is a loud ringing sound. The ode's irregular, Pindaric stanzas, of different lengths and metres, were designed to give the composer contrasting movements; Bray's study shows how closely Draghi followed these shifts. Such onomatopoeia was much admired by eighteenth-century readers.

title: complaining flute ... warbling lute
short: The flute (the recorder, in 1687) 'complains' (laments) and 'discovers' (reveals) the sorrows of hopeless lovers.
body: In Restoration England 'flute' normally meant the recorder, an instrument associated with love and mourning. 'Complaining' has the sense of the literary 'complaint', a lament; 'discovers' means reveals. 'Dying notes' plays on the fading sound and on the lover's 'death'. The stanza is a single sentence of four lines whose soft liquids and long vowels contrast with the drumming consonants of the stanza before.

title: Sharp violins
short: The violin, still a relatively new and bright-toned instrument in English music, voices jealousy and fury in a tumble of feminine rhymes.
body: Charles II had formed a band of twenty-four violins on the French model, and the violin family was displacing the softer viols. 'Sharp' describes its bright, cutting tone and perhaps its high pitch. The stanza's rhymes on '-ation' and '-ion' (desperation, indignation, passion) and its list structure create a frantic effect. 'The fair, disdainful dame' is the cruel mistress of love poetry.

title: the sacred organ ... mend the choirs above
short: The organ, the instrument of church music and of St Cecilia, surpasses all others because it inspires 'holy love' and joins the heavenly choirs.
body: After instruments of war and earthly love, stanza 6 rises to sacred music. 'Mend' here means to improve or augment (OED), so the organ's notes travel upward to add to the angelic choirs: a bold compliment, since heavenly music should need no mending. The progression from secular to sacred structures the ode and prepares for Cecilia, traditionally (and anachronistically) credited with inventing the organ.

anchor: Orpheus could lead the savage race
title: Orpheus ... Sequacious of the lyre
short: Orpheus' music drew wild beasts and uprooted trees after him; Cecilia's achievement is greater still because it draws an angel down.
body: In Ovid (Metamorphoses 10.86-105 and 11.1-2) trees and beasts gather to hear Orpheus. 'Sequacious' (from Latin sequax, following) is a learned Latinism meaning inclined to follow (OED); the rare word gives the uprooted trees a faintly comic docility, as if they were disciples. The comparison between pagan and Christian musicians is a set piece of Cecilian odes: Orpheus moved nature, Cecilia moves heaven, and the stanza's rising lines enact that ascent from earth to the angelic.

title: An angel heard ... Mistaking earth for heaven
short: In legend an angel visited the martyr Cecilia; Dryden wittily makes the angel come because her organ music made earth sound like heaven.
body: The legend of St Cecilia (an early Roman martyr, in versions such as the Golden Legend and Chaucer's Second Nun's Tale) tells that an angel guarded her chastity and appeared to her and her husband Valerian. Dryden transforms the story into a compliment to music: when breath was given to her organ (the air in its pipes), an angel 'straight appear'd', deceived into thinking he heard heaven. The witty conceit recalls Jubal's brethren mistaking a shell for a god, and it raises 'the wonder higher' than Orpheus.

anchor: And Music shall untune the sky
title: Grand Chorus: untune the sky
short: The music of the spheres began the world and the last trumpet will end it: music that tuned creation will finally 'untune' it at the Judgement.
body: The spheres were thought to move to divine music, singing the Creator's praise. At the Last Judgement 'the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised' (1 Corinthians 15:52); the earthly 'pageant' (a show, a stage-spectacle, with an echo of The Tempest's 'insubstantial pageant') will crumble. The final paradox, that music shall 'untune' the sky, has divided readers: Johnson, in his Life of Dryden, called the conclusion striking but wished the antithesis of music 'untuning' had found some other place; Hollander took the line for the title of his book. The line 'The dead shall live, the living die' is a chiasmus imitating that reversal.
